oppose_rescission_weaken_cra.label: Oppose rescinding or weakening CRA
oppose_rescission_weaken_cra.definition: General opposition to rescinding the 2023 rule and weakening CRA accountability, transparency and community obligations, including claims it benefits banks over communities.

support_proposal_burden_relief.label: Support proposal and burden reduction
support_proposal_burden_relief.definition: Support for rescission and for simplifying CRA, cutting compliance cost, recordkeeping and complexity, especially for community banks.

withdraw_or_delay_proposal.label: Withdraw, delay or reissue proposal
withdraw_or_delay_proposal.definition: Calls to withdraw, suspend, restart or delay the rulemaking, including pending impact analysis or recent housing legislation.

comment_period_process.label: Comment period and procedural concerns
comment_period_process.definition: Requests to extend the comment period and concerns about APA notice, insufficient information, proposal complexity and unexplained departure from the 2023 rule.

lack_of_impact_analysis.label: Lack of impact and cost-benefit analysis
lack_of_impact_analysis.definition: Criticism that agencies did not analyze effects on LMI, rural, minority and redlined communities, housing and lending, or that cost and paperwork estimates were flawed.

interagency_inconsistency_fed.label: Interagency inconsistency and Fed absence
interagency_inconsistency_fed.definition: Concerns about divergent rules across OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve, repeated rule changes, instability, and calls for a uniform, durable interagency rule.

asset_size_thresholds.label: Asset size thresholds for bank categories
asset_size_thresholds.definition: Positions on raising, keeping or indexing thresholds for small, intermediate and large banks, including $1B, $3.252B, $10B and $30B options.

bank_reclassification_loss_of_coverage.label: Banks reclassified and losing CRA obligations
bank_reclassification_loss_of_coverage.definition: Concerns that raised thresholds move banks into lighter categories, removing tests, data reporting and local obligations, including branchless or digital banks.

investment_test_cd_tests.label: Investment test and CD evaluation for banks
investment_test_cd_tests.definition: Concerns about eliminating the standalone investment test and weakening community development tests for large and intermediate banks.

cd_benchmarks_strategic_plans.label: CD benchmarks and strategic plan option
cd_benchmarks_strategic_plans.definition: Views on the 0.625% Tier 1 capital benchmark, other quantitative benchmarks becoming ceilings, and strategic plan guardrails, process and public participation.

economic_dev_infrastructure_eligibility.label: Broadened economic development and infrastructure credit
economic_dev_infrastructure_eligibility.definition: Concerns about removing the economic development purpose test and crediting infrastructure or other activities with little LMI benefit.

cd_definitions_eligible_activities.label: CD definitions, NOAH and qualifying activities
cd_definitions_eligible_activities.definition: Comments on defining and adding qualifying activities such as NOAH, SBA 504, CDFIs, disaster resilience, special purpose credit programs, financial education and illustrative lists.

confirmation_transition_implementation.label: Confirmation process and implementation timing
confirmation_transition_implementation.definition: Comments on advance confirmation of activities, examiner guidance, effective dates, transition periods and treatment of prior-period or pending commitments.

grant_indirect_cost_cap.label: 15% indirect cost cap on grants
grant_indirect_cost_cap.definition: Objections to or comments on the 15 percent cap on indirect or overhead costs for grants receiving CRA credit, including definitions and calculation base.

grant_eligibility_documentation.label: Grant eligibility and documentation burden
grant_eligibility_documentation.definition: Concerns about limits on credit for general operating, capacity-building and other grants, and documentation burdens that lead banks to cut or redirect grants away from small nonprofits.

nonprofit_cdfi_partnerships.label: Impacts on CDFIs, nonprofits and partnerships
nonprofit_cdfi_partnerships.definition: Importance of CRA incentives for bank capital, grants and partnerships with CDFIs, nonprofits, intermediaries and mission-driven lenders, and effects of losing them.

affordable_housing_lihtc_effects.label: Affordable housing and LIHTC/NMTC investment effects
affordable_housing_lihtc_effects.definition: Concerns that weakened CRA reduces bank demand and pricing for LIHTC, Housing Credit and NMTC equity and reduces affordable housing production and funding.

reduced_cd_activity_overall.label: Reduced community development activity overall
reduced_cd_activity_overall.definition: Projected declines in bank community development lending, investment and services and weaker incentives for private capital flow.

service_test_deposit_branches.label: Service test, deposit products and branches
service_test_deposit_branches.definition: Concerns about dropping deposit products and narrowing retail services review, branch closures and deserts, and access for unbanked and underbanked households.

assessment_areas_outside_aa.label: Assessment areas and credit outside them
assessment_areas_outside_aa.definition: Comments on assessment area definitions, geographic flexibility, credit for community development outside assessment areas, digital banking and CRA deserts.

retail_lending_major_product_lines.label: Retail lending test and major product lines
retail_lending_major_product_lines.definition: Comments on limiting review to top product lines, consumer lending evaluation, complexity definitions, purpose test for small business loans, and risk of hiding lending gaps.

data_reporting_transparency.label: CRA data collection, reporting and transparency
data_reporting_transparency.definition: Concerns about losing small business, small farm, community development and other CRA data, Section 1071 overlap, and public visibility into lending gaps.

fair_lending_redlining_enforcement.label: Fair lending, redlining and discrimination evidence
fair_lending_redlining_enforcement.definition: Concerns about narrowing discrimination evidence for rating downgrades, redlining accountability, consumer protection enforcement and merger or consolidation review.

harm_lmi_minority_communities.label: Harm to LMI, minority and underserved communities
harm_lmi_minority_communities.definition: General concerns and CRA's anti-redlining purpose, with impacts on LMI, minority, disabled and limited-English people, small businesses and local communities.

rural_tribal_disaster_impacts.label: Rural, Tribal and disaster-area impacts
rural_tribal_disaster_impacts.definition: Effects on rural and small communities and requests to recognize Indian Country, Indian Housing Plans, Tribal engagement and disaster areas.

small_business_lending.label: Small business lending and SBA programs
small_business_lending.definition: Comments on small business credit gaps, SBA 504 and SBA-aligned thresholds, revenue thresholds and technical assistance.

extend_cra_nonbanks.label: Extending CRA to nonbanks and credit unions
extend_cra_nonbanks.definition: Calls to cover credit unions, fintechs and other nonbanks under CRA.

off_topic.label: Off-topic or irrelevant comments
off_topic.definition: Comments unrelated to the CRA rule, such as fraud claims, remittance taxes, digital currency or personal disputes.

other.label: Other issues
other.definition: Issues that fit none of the canonical issues.

comments.name: Kenneth Thomas
comments.type_basis: Submitted under his own name with no organization listed, writing from personal experience and describing himself as an individual submitter.
comments.overall_quote: The July 31, 2026 OCC/FDIC CRA proposal, OCC-2026-0694, is very disappointing because it fails to address the central reason CRA modernization became necessary in the first place
comments.summary: The commenter objects that the proposal keeps CRA assessment areas tied to physical branches. He says this leaves communities that supply deposits to branchless and digital banks without a reinvestment obligation, a problem he calls "weblining." He urges the agencies to adopt a deposit-based assessment area rule with a 5 percent threshold, modeled on the OCC's 2020 rule. He also suggests a simple approach: keep the 1995 regulations and add that rule plus useful elements of the 2023 rule.
key_asks: Request comment on a targeted deposit-based assessment-area framework, including a modern 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule like the OCC's 2020 rule.
Keep the 1995 regulations and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule.
Add the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 rule, such as the list of qualified CD activities.

provisions.quote: By retaining a framework centered on physical facilities, the proposal misses an important opportunity to modernize CRA for the realities of digital banking.
maintain the current 1995 regs and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule and the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 CRA Final Rule

comments.commenter_subtype: private individual (former Senate staff/economist, Ph.D.)

sources.quote: like my home community of South Florida

issues.raw_label: Failure to address digital banking
issues.quote: it fails to address the central reason CRA modernization became necessary in the first place: the growth of digital and branchless banking since CRA’s last major reform in 1995.

issues.raw_label: Deposit-based assessment areas needed
issues.quote: the OCC and FDIC should reconsider this serious omission and specifically request comment on a targeted deposit-based assessment-area framework

issues.raw_label: 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule
issues.quote: a bank has a CRA reinvestment requirement in any area sourcing 5% or more of its deposits.

issues.raw_label: Branchless banks escaping CRA obligations
issues.quote: leaves those communities without a corresponding CRA reinvestment obligation.

issues.raw_label: Weblining of deposits from communities
issues.quote: the comparable danger is what I have labeled "weblining," namely the ability of branchless banks to gather substantial deposits electronically from communities

issues.raw_label: South Florida deposits without reinvestment
issues.quote: There is no commensurate reinvestment requirement for the more than $100 billion of estimated deposits these branchless banks harvest from South Florida.

issues.raw_label: Retain 2020 OCC deposit-based approach
issues.quote: Comptroller Otting’s 2020 OCC rule demonstrated that this problem can be addressed in a targeted manner with deposit-based assessment area

issues.raw_label: Maintain 1995 regs with updates
issues.quote: maintain the current 1995 regs and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule and the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 CRA Final Rule

comments.name: San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative
comments.type_basis: Self-described regional nonprofit whose members include affordable housing developers, local governments, lenders, and community organizations in California's San Joaquin Valley.
comments.overall_quote: We recognize and support the agencies' goals of clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for community banks. But these two provisions would not reduce burden on communities.
comments.summary: The Collaborative, a San Joaquin Valley housing nonprofit, objects to two provisions: reclassifying banks between $1.65B and $10B as intermediate banks outside the investment test, and the limits on CD grants including the 15 percent overhead documentation. It argues these would reduce LIHTC investment and grant support in a capital-scarce region, while voicing general support for clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for community banks.
key_asks: Retain a community development investment component for banks above the current large bank threshold, or at minimum give LIHTC and other CD investments distinct, meaningful recognition in the intermediate bank evaluation.
Withdraw the 15 percent overhead documentation requirement for CD grants.
Preserve CRA consideration for grants, including general operating support, to organizations with a community development purpose.

provisions.quote: If these banks can receive the same CRA consideration for ordinary market-rate lending, many will have little reason to continue purchasing housing credits.
The 15 percent overhead figure has no basis in how effective nonprofits actually operate, and it penalizes small rural organizations that run lean

comments.name: For Small Business Only LLC
comments.type_basis: The commenter describes itself as a Virginia LLC acting as a technical-assistance and capital-readiness intermediary for small businesses, working with nonprofits and banks.
comments.overall_quote: For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the agencies' proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations.
comments.summary: The commenter, a small-business technical-assistance and capital-readiness intermediary, strongly supports the proposal. It focuses on the recognition of technical assistance, financial literacy, direct nonprofit grants with assessment-area nexus, and the 15% indirect-cost cap. It asks for implementation clarifications on grant documentation, including for new nonprofits, curriculum licensing fees, reporting costs and related-party safeguards.
key_asks: Retain the economic development category covering technical assistance for small businesses and farms, and preserve the 15% indirect-cost guardrail in the final rule.

Clarify the 15% grant rules: allow newly formed nonprofits without a Form 990 to document compliance through budgets, policies and attestation. Treat arm's-length curriculum license fees and outcome-reporting costs as direct costs. Allow related-party costs with safeguards. Confirm that 2 CFR part 200-comparable cost allocation methods are acceptable.
Encourage a standardized but scalable evidence package for grant recipients, and keep making clear that technical assistance does not require or guarantee a subsequent loan.

provisions.quote: FSBO supports the proposed 15% indirect-cost limit for community-development grants made by large banks.
FSBO particularly supports the proposed economic-development category covering technical assistance and support services for qualifying small businesses and farms.

comments.name: T.R.U.S.T. South LA
comments.type_basis: The letter describes the organization as a community-based nonprofit that creates permanently affordable housing and stewards community land trusts in South Los Angeles.
comments.overall_quote: We respectfully urge the FDIC and OCC to reject these proposed changes
comments.summary: T.R.U.S.T. South LA, a South Los Angeles affordable housing nonprofit, strongly opposes the proposal. It argues the changes would cut community development investment, branches and deposit services, data transparency, nonprofit grants, and accountability for discrimination. It also asks for a 60-day extension and stronger Tribal provisions.
key_asks: Reject the proposed changes and keep strong CRA obligations, including not raising asset thresholds.
Extend the comment period by 60 days and analyze the impact on LMI communities.
Add Tribal engagement incentives, preserve the 15% overhead and grant flexibility for nonprofits, and consider all evidence of discrimination in ratings.

provisions.quote: Asset thresholds should not be raised.
Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal policy and practice
The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.
CRA rules should also expand the definition of assessment areas to include areas where banks conduct substantial lending
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made
Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings.
The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs
Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment.
Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little benefit.

comments.name: South Carolina Association for Community Economic Development (SCACED)
comments.type_basis: The author leads SCACED, a coalition of member organizations that build wealth in under-resourced neighborhoods through housing, small business support and workforce training.
comments.overall_quote: I find this proposal deeply concerning.

He argues it would cut bank community development lending, investment and grants, remove community development obligations for about a quarter of South Carolina banks, and cost the state bank branches in low- and moderate-income areas. comments.overall_quote: we urge the agencies to ensure that the proposed changes do not unintentionally weaken bank accountability or reduce investment in communities that continue to experience barriers to credit and capital.
comments.summary: The Greater Baltimore Urban League acknowledges the agencies' goals of reducing burden but urges that the changes not weaken accountability or reduce investment in underserved communities. It objects specifically to the 15% indirect-cost limit on CD grants and asks the agencies to preserve CRA credit for small-business support, workforce, housing and financial empowerment activities, and to keep transparency.

Maintain transparent and accountable evaluation standards that reflect local community needs

comments.type_basis: The letter describes SBCLT as a community-based nonprofit in Santa Clara County that preserves permanently affordable housing through community ownership.
comments.overall_quote: The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities
comments.summary: South Bay Community Land Trust, an affordable housing nonprofit, strongly opposes the proposal. It argues the rule would sharply cut community development finance, branches, deposit products, data and nonprofit grants, and would weaken the response to discrimination, and it says the agencies did not analyze these impacts. It requests a 60-day comment extension and offers specific alternatives, including Tribal-focused provisions and tighter NOAH credit conditions.
key_asks: Extend the comment period by 60 days and have the agencies analyze the expected loss of CRA activity.
Do not raise asset thresholds, and keep the deposit services, grant eligibility, purpose test and discrimination provisions that protect LMI communities.
Add an impact and responsiveness review factor on bank engagement with Tribes and allow out-of-assessment-area credit for activity benefiting Tribes.

provisions.quote: Asset thresholds should not be raised.
the 15% overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success
The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.
CRA rules should also expand the definition of assessment areas to include areas where banks conduct substantial lending
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made
Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings.
The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of economic development.
Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment.
Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
a problem the regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA Rule
Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little benefit.

comments.overall_quote: The Housing Advisory Group strongly recommends and encourages the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule.
comments.summary: The Housing Advisory Group, an affordable housing developer association, opposes raising the asset thresholds. It argues that dropping the investment test for banks reclassified as intermediate would cut demand and competition for LIHTC equity and create investment deserts, especially in rural areas. It calls the $30 billion alternative the most damaging and the $3.252 billion alternative less disruptive, and it asks that the thresholds stay as they are.
key_asks: Leave the asset thresholds as they stand under the 1995 CRA rule.
If changes proceed, keep the lowest possible large bank threshold, such as the $3.252 billion alternative rather than $10 billion or $30 billion.
Keep the investment requirement, as well as lending, for newly designated intermediate banks.

provisions.quote: What will have a significant impact on affordable housing production is the elimination of the investment test for these banks.
This alternative would be substantially less disruptive to LIHTC investment than the primary proposal to raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

comments.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
comments.type_basis: Letter is submitted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's Center for Capital Markets Competitiveness, a business trade association, on behalf of its members.
comments.overall_quote: While the NPRM provides critical regulatory relief and appropriately respects key statutory guardrails, other elements of the proposal threaten to unnecessarily disrupt the historically proven 1995 framework.

comments.name: RMCRC (Rocky Mountain Community Reinvestment Corporation)
comments.type_basis: The comment states RMCRC is a 501(c)(3) CDFI specializing in permanent debt financing of multi-family affordable housing.
comments.overall_quote: We support several elements of the proposal.
comments.summary: RMCRC, a national affordable housing CDFI funded by bank partners, supports the clarification that multi-family affordable housing qualifies and the consortium or third-party CD loan mechanism. It worries that higher asset thresholds, weaker intermediate bank CD obligations, the assessment-area-first approach to outside-area credit, and the 15 percent grant overhead cap would reduce bank capital for CDFIs and affordable rental housing, and it asks for modifications.
key_asks: Retain a meaningful standalone community development performance expectation for intermediate banks.
Allow CRA consideration outside assessment areas for CD financing through certified national or multi-state CDFIs, with a safe harbor or presumptive treatment.
Apply any indirect cost limit on grants flexibly rather than as a bright line, and preserve CD lending data and publish an affordable housing impact analysis.

provisions.quote: the proposed asset size thresholds, the changes to intermediate bank ratings, and the cap on indirect costs for community development grants would sharply reduce the capital that flows from banks to CDFIs
a rigid assessment area first framework can create an unintended mismatch between where a bank's CRA obligations arise and where affordable housing capital is most needed.
the proposed 15 percent limitation on indirect administrative costs could unintentionally reduce support for nonprofit and CDFI infrastructure.
Maintain meaningful data and transparency regarding community development lending
the proposal to provide a mechanism for CRA consideration of qualifying community development loans originated or purchased through a consortium or third party.
we support the proposed clarification that multi-family affordable housing can qualify as community development

comments.name: Project Read (joint letter with Elevate Utah and Wasatch Homeless Health Care dba Fourth Street Clinic)
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by leaders of Utah nonprofits (Project Read, Elevate Utah, Fourth Street Clinic) that describe themselves as nonprofits serving low- and moderate-income Utahns and receiving CRA grants.
comments.overall_quote: We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap or substantially revise it to recognize legitimate, reasonable, and federally accepted nonprofit cost structures.
comments.summary: Three Utah nonprofits argue that the proposed 15% indirect-cost ceiling on community-development grant recipients misuses the federal de minimis rate. They say it would push banks to favor larger organizations over small local nonprofits, create undefined measurement and compliance burdens, and conflict with the Federal Reserve's standards. They ask the agencies to remove the cap or substantially revise it, and they use Project Read as an example.
key_asks: Remove the fixed 15% indirect-cost ceiling on community-development grant recipients, or if one is kept, define indirect costs and the measurement base clearly.

If a standard is retained, add a safe harbor for smaller nonprofits, keep CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants, reduce documentation burdens, and provide a transition period for multi-year grants.
Coordinate with the Federal Reserve Board to keep a consistent interagency standard for community-development grants, or explain how the agencies will handle the divergence.

provisions.quote: We respectfully ask the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed fixed 15% indirect-cost ceiling.

comments.commenter_subtype: Utah nonprofit organizations (adult literacy provider and community health clinic coalition)

issues.quote: Clearly define "indirect costs" and the applicable measurement base, so that nonprofits and banks can apply the standard consistently.

comments.name: American Fintech Council
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by AFC's Chief Policy Officer and describes AFC as a trade association of more than 150 fintech companies and innovative banks.
comments.overall_quote: The Proposed Rule advances several of those objectives. However, AFC recognizes that several of the changes under consideration by the Proposed Rule could adversely affect the CRA efforts of innovative banks
comments.summary: AFC, a fintech and innovative bank trade group, welcomes the proposal's aims of flexibility and reduced burden but asks for changes so that it does not harm innovative banks. It urges keeping the limited purpose bank designation and flexible strategic plans, a materiality-based major product line test, a safe harbor for the 15 percent grant cap, flexible outside-assessment-area community development credit, and streamlined data reporting.
key_asks: Preserve the limited purpose bank designation, treat the 5 percent incidental lending threshold as a rebuttable presumption, and keep strategic plans flexible with transition and grandfathering treatment.

Adopt a materiality-based major product line framework, restore the loan-to-deposit ratio language on other lending-related activities, and avoid adverse conclusions for nationwide or digital models with few in-area loans.

Treat the 15 percent indirect cost limit as a safe harbor, keep a flexible and attainable outside-assessment-area community development pathway, and align data reporting with Section 1071 and with sufficient implementation time.

provisions.quote: AFC strongly recommends that the agencies preserve the limited purpose (LP) bank designation.

AFC recognizes that the Proposed Rule would not provide for the assessment of deposit products, consistent with the agencies' position in pending litigation, and does not ask the agencies to revisit that position.
AFC recognizes the agencies' position that the CRA does not permit assessment of retail lending outside those areas and does not ask the agencies to extend CRA consideration to such lending.
The final rule should preserve a practical pathway for banks to receive CRA consideration for qualifying community development activities outside their facility-based assessment areas
AFC recommends that the agencies treat the proposed 15 percent indirect cost threshold as a safe harbor rather than an absolute limitation
an institution should not be required to collect and report information unless that information materially contributes to its CRA evaluation or serves a distinct and identifiable supervisory purpose.

provisions.quote: The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA.

The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets

comments.name: Evernorth
comments.type_basis: Evernorth describes itself as a mission-driven LIHTC syndicator and community development organization created by state housing finance agencies in Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont.
comments.overall_quote: Evernorth respectfully urges the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to retain the current Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) asset thresholds.
comments.summary: Evernorth, a LIHTC syndicator in Northern New England, opposes raising the CRA asset thresholds. It says reclassifying banks would reduce Housing Credit equity, including through multi-investor fund ownership limits, and it urges retaining the current thresholds or, failing that, adopting the $3.252 billion alternative. It also supports workforce housing credit only if affordability protections stay in place and LMI housing remains the focus.
key_asks: Retain the current Large and Small Bank asset thresholds; if the Large Bank threshold is raised, adopt the $3.252 billion alternative rather than $10 billion, and reject the $30 billion and $10 billion Small Bank options.
Keep the requirement that Intermediate Banks achieve at least satisfactory on both Lending and Community Development tests for an overall satisfactory rating.
Assess reclassification effects on multi-investor funds as a whole, including constraints on remaining investors' commitments.

provisions.quote: Evernorth strongly recommends against adopting a $30 billion Large Bank threshold.
Evernorth recommends continuing to require Intermediate Banks to demonstrate satisfactory performance in both Lending and Community Development to receive an overall satisfactory rating.

Evernorth supports using CRA to address workforce housing needs in high-cost areas, as long as protections keep that housing affordable and strong incentives remain in place for investment in housing serving LMI households.

comments.overall_quote: Our organization encourages the OCC and FDIC to rescind this proposal so as to prevent a decline in CRA-related investment activity.
comments.summary: A coalition of Capital Region (NY) housing and community development nonprofits, including a CDFI, opposes the proposal as weakening bank accountability in low- and moderate-income communities. It objects to the higher asset thresholds, reduced reporting, removal of deposit account evaluation, the 15 percent grant overhead limit and documentation, and elimination of the economic development purpose test, and asks the agencies to rescind the proposal.
key_asks: Rescind the proposal and do not weaken CRA regulations
Keep evaluation of deposit accounts and reward branch opening while penalizing closures in underserved areas
Retain the economic development purpose test and do not raise asset thresholds or reduce reporting

provisions.quote: Reclassifying banks as small and intermediate banks would reduce community reinvestment activity.
Proposing to remove evaluation of checking and deposit accounts would be detrimental to our efforts to find good products for our clients
Requiring that bank grants limit operating costs to less than 15 percent and requiring new documentation is an additional obstacle for banks and community groups.
Removing the "purpose test" from bank economic development activity significantly weakens the Community Reinvestment Act.
Reducing reporting requirements makes it difficult to compare bank performance for underserved populations.
Access to physical banking is still essential for LMI people, communities and small businesses.

comments.commenter_subtype: community development coalition (housing counseling, CDFI, land trust, tenant organizations)

issues.quote: Rigorous CRA reports help communities identify lending gaps.

issues.raw_label: Removing evaluation of deposit accounts

issues.quote: Prioritize the opening of branches and penalize the closing of branches in underserved areas.

issues.raw_label: Bank grant operating cost cap and documentation
issues.quote: Requiring that bank grants limit operating costs to less than 15 percent and requiring new documentation is an additional obstacle for banks and community groups.

issues.raw_label: Removing the purpose test
issues.quote: Removing the "purpose test" from bank economic development activity significantly weakens the Community Reinvestment Act.

issues.raw_label: Rescind the proposal entirely
issues.quote: Our organization encourages the OCC and FDIC to rescind this proposal so as to prevent a decline in CRA-related investment activity.

comments.name: Partners for Rural Transformation
comments.type_basis: The letter describes PRT as a coalition of six CDFIs serving rural and Native persistent-poverty communities.
comments.overall_quote: While we broadly support the idea of greater clarity and reduced burden, the proposed changes miss the opportunity to strengthen incentives in rural and Tribal regions experiencing persistent poverty
comments.summary: PRT, a coalition of rural and Native CDFIs, opposes the higher asset thresholds and the limits on CD grants. It says these changes would cut bank community development investment in persistent-poverty rural and Tribal areas. It also asks for a faster eligibility response window, retention of the Native Land Area framework, and transparency for strategic plans, while welcoming the illustrative activity list and expanded large-bank reporting.
key_asks: Maintain the current asset thresholds for small, intermediate, and large banks.
Keep grants in the community development definition and remove the 15% administrative cost cap.
Retain the 2023 Native Land Area framework, require limited-purpose bank ratings to consider service to disadvantaged areas, and set a 10-business-day response window for CD eligibility inquiries.

provisions.quote: Partners for Rural Transformation recommend that the regulators maintain the current asset thresholds.
keep grants in the Community Development investment definition and remove the 15% cap on administrative costs.

The proposed change to the strategic plan option has potential to be a meaningful vehicle to bring bank investment into rural, Tribal and persistent poverty communities, but only with accountability and transparency.
we appreciate the expanded reporting for large banks that the proposal suggests
PRT welcomes the proposal's recommendation to publish an illustrative list of activities eligible for Community Development consideration
Removing this factor when calculating a rating shifts focus away from the places with the greatest need for access to fair credit.

comments.name: Association for Enterprise Opportunity
comments.type_basis: AEO describes itself as a 35-year-old national association supporting entrepreneurs, CDFIs, nonprofit lenders and business-support organizations.
comments.overall_quote: We are concerned, however, that several proposed changes could reduce the incentives, information, and institutional capacity that connect very small businesses and underserved entrepreneurs to responsible capital.
comments.summary: AEO supports proportionate regulation but opposes the proposal's higher asset thresholds, rigid 15 percent indirect-cost ceiling, and any elimination of grants. It asks for a flexible grant standard, protection of technical assistance and intermediaries, continued visibility of small-business lending, and reliable public data.
key_asks: Use a more moderate asset threshold (no higher than $3.252B) and preserve a meaningful community development test for reclassified banks
Retain grants and donations; treat 15 percent as a safe harbor with flexible, documented indirect-cost standards and protect capacity-building and intermediary grants
Keep material small-business lending visible in evaluations and preserve CRA small-business data until Section 1071 data are fully usable

provisions.quote: The agencies should reject the 30 billion dollar option and should not adopt the proposed 10 billion dollar large-bank threshold without substantial safeguards.
We oppose the proposed 15 percent ceiling as an all-or-nothing condition for CRA consideration.
AEO supports eliminating true duplication, but only after the replacement data are fully operational
banks should first demonstrate that they are meeting needs in their assessment areas.
AEO supports clearer definitions, a timely process for confirming whether an activity will receive CRA consideration, standardized public information

comments.name: Cinnaire
comments.type_basis: Cinnaire describes itself as a Michigan-based organization raising capital for affordable housing, using LIHTC, NMTC and CDFI lending, with an affiliated certified CDFI.
comments.overall_quote: The NPR includes changes to the CRA regulatory framework that could negatively impact LIHTC investment, especially in rural communities that struggle to attract LIHTC capital.
comments.summary: Cinnaire, an affordable housing capital raiser and CDFI affiliate, says raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion would remove the standalone investment test for hundreds of banks and hurt rural LIHTC investment. It recommends a $3.252 billion threshold if any increase occurs, opposes $30 billion, and cautions against new grant restrictions. It supports credit for prior-period CD loans and a public illustrative list of eligible activities.
key_asks: If the large bank threshold is raised, adopt the $3.252 billion alternative rather than $10 billion, and reject $30 billion.
Retain the requirement that intermediate banks earn at least Satisfactory on the CD test to get an overall Satisfactory rating.
Maintain current CRA eligibility for CD grants, and create a public, illustrative list of eligible CD activities with advance confirmation.

provisions.quote: We fear that this threshold could inadvertently undermine the LIHTC program's ability to respond to the housing crisis, especially in rural areas that should be prioritized for affordable housing investment.
We also strongly oppose a $30 billion large bank threshold, which would have even more significant negative impacts.
We encourage regulators to adopt strong quantitative and qualitative approaches to ensure that banks first meet the needs of their assessment areas
we caution against imposing new and burdensome restrictions on banks and community partners, which would increase costs and regulatory complexity.

comments.commenter_subtype: CDFI and affordable housing finance organization (LIHTC syndicator with affiliated CDFI lender)

sources.quote: Cinnaire is a Michigan-based organization working to raise capital for affordable housing

comments.name: Sonoma County Community Development Commission
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by the Executive Director of the Sonoma County Community Development Commission, which describes itself as a governmental agency.
comments.overall_quote: We are concerned that several elements of the proposed revisions could reduce the availability of this critical support, particularly for lower-income households and communities with the greatest housing needs.
comments.summary: A county housing and community development agency warns that higher asset thresholds, limits on CRA credit for grants, a looser affordable housing definition, and a low local community development minimum would reduce bank investment in LIHTC, housing bonds, and nonprofit support. It asks the agencies to keep strong CRA incentives, recognize operating and capacity grants, preserve durable income-based affordability, and study cumulative effects before finalizing.
key_asks: Avoid raising asset thresholds so that banks remain subject to meaningful community development and investment evaluation, preserving incentives for LIHTC and affordable housing bonds.
Continue CRA consideration for general operating support, capacity building, intermediary and collaborative grants.
Keep an income-sensitive affordable housing definition with enforceable long-term affordability, and assess the cumulative effects on housing capital and nonprofit capacity before finalizing.

provisions.quote: Raising the threshold for full CRA requirements from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets—and potentially to $30 billion—could reduce incentives for a significant number of banks
Restricting CRA credit to grants that are directly tied to a specific community development program could exclude essential operating support, capacity-building grants
the minimum could become a practical benchmark rather than a floor for institutions that currently provide greater support.
allowing unsubsidized, market-rate apartments to qualify as affordable housing based on current rents, without adequate protections for continued affordability, could divert investment

comments.name: Monica Cruz
comments.type_basis: She writes as a board member of Esperanza Community Land Trust, a San Antonio affordable housing nonprofit.
comments.overall_quote: I am writing to express my strong support for maintaining a robust and effective Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
comments.summary: A board member of a San Antonio community land trust urges regulators to keep a strong CRA that incentivizes affordable housing development and preservation. She asks the agencies to reconsider the higher asset thresholds and to protect nonprofit access to CRA grants, including reasonable operating expenses. She does not explicitly address the rescission, and the grants provision is not named, so that position is inferred from her text on nonprofit expenses.
key_asks: Reconsider the proposed asset-size thresholds and assess their impact on communities, nonprofits and affordable housing providers before making changes.
Preserve the full range of CRA community development activities (lending, grants, investments) without favoring one over another.
Protect nonprofit access to CRA-supported grants and investments, recognizing reasonable administrative and operating expenses.

provisions.quote: I urge regulators to carefully reconsider proposed asset-size thresholds that would reduce the number of banks subject to more comprehensive CRA evaluations.
Reasonable administrative and operating expenses are necessary to effectively manage programs, serve residents, and ensure long-term success.

Use asset-based rather than capital-based CD benchmarks, such as a 1% of assets rule of thumb.

I continue to support the challenge to the 2023 CRA Final Rule.

Nor do the current NPR's proposed Community Development (CD) metrics work.

comments.name: Valley National Bank
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by Valley National Bank's EVP and Chief CSR-CRA Officer. It describes Valley as an OCC-supervised national bank with over $66 billion in assets.
comments.overall_quote: Certain provisions in the NPR, if applied too rigidly, could unintentionally reduce the flow of credit, investments, grants, services, and nonprofit support to LMI individuals, small businesses, affordable housing providers, and underserved communities.
comments.summary: Valley National Bank, an OCC-supervised bank, supports CRA's core mission and parts of the proposal's clarity goals. It objects to the grant indirect-cost limit and the removal of deposit services. It also asks for several technical changes: average Tier 1 capital, Option 2 for outside-AA flexibility, Option 1 for product lines, counting CD loan renewals, interagency alignment, and a transition period. The letter does not directly address the rescission of the 2023 rule.

Use average quarterly Tier 1 capital, adopt Option 2 for geographic flexibility and Option 1 for major product lines, count CD loan renewals, and align with the Federal Reserve.

Valley recommends retaining consideration for deposit products and alternative delivery systems that demonstrate a meaningful connection to credit access, credit readiness
supports the qualitative framework reflected in Option 2, which evaluates whether a bank has adequately served its assessment areas over the full evaluation period
clear and stable asset thresholds are an important part of an effective framework because they recognize differences in bank size and business models
The final rule should provide flexibility to allow examiners to consider customer behavior, digital access, and community activity centers when assessing meaningful access to banking services.
Valley supports the institution-level approach reflected in Option 1 for identifying a bank's major retail product lines.

comments.name: Council for Affordable and Rural Housing (CARH)
comments.type_basis: CARH describes itself as an association representing for-profit and nonprofit developers, owners, and lenders of affordable rural rental housing.
comments.overall_quote: CARH supports the Agencies' efforts to make the CRA clearer, more consistent, and more workable for institutions of different sizes
comments.summary: CARH, a rural affordable housing association, supports the goal of simplifying CRA but warns that raising asset thresholds and loosening intermediate bank community development requirements would reduce bank Housing Credit investment in rural areas. It urges a $3.252 billion large bank threshold at most, welcomes outside assessment area credit, opposes new grant documentation limits, and asks for explicit recognition of USDA rural housing programs.
key_asks: If the large bank threshold is raised, adopt the $3.252 billion alternative rather than $10 billion; reject the $30 billion large bank threshold and a $10 billion small bank threshold.
Retain the requirement that intermediate banks achieve at least Satisfactory community development performance for an overall Satisfactory rating.
Expressly recognize Housing Credit, USDA Section 514/515/538, MPR and SARA preservation activities as CRA-eligible, and keep affordable housing credit focused on LMI households.

provisions.quote: CARH strongly opposes a $30 billion large bank threshold.

Finalize the rule jointly with the Federal Reserve, or allow a longer effective date.

comments.name: U.S. Impact Investing Alliance
comments.type_basis: The Alliance describes itself as an organization promoting impact investing, whose community includes family offices, foundations, CDFIs, fund managers and institutional asset allocators.
comments.overall_quote: the proposal as a whole would substantially narrow the CRA's reach.
comments.summary: The Alliance, an impact investing organization, opposes much of the proposal because it would remove community development expectations from about 800 banks and the investment test from about 375 more. This would reduce the anchor capital that CDFIs, LIHTC and NMTC investors, and impact co-investors depend on. It also objects to the grant limits, the removal of the purpose test, the low geographic flexibility benchmark, the strategic plan changes and the litigation request, while supporting some clarity-oriented elements.

Retain the economic development purpose test and a meaningful benefit requirement for infrastructure, and do not adopt the 15 percent grant cap or eliminate grants
Publish an analysis of effects by state and activity, extend the comment period, and withdraw the request for a court judgment limiting future rulemaking

Physical facilities should not be treated as the outer boundary of a bank's community

comments.name: UnidosUS
comments.type_basis: Describes itself as the nation's largest Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization with an affiliate network of nearly 300 community-based organizations.
comments.overall_quote: UnidosUS urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this proposal because it would weaken community development obligations, reduce the number of institutions subject to meaningful CRA oversight, narrow geographic accountability, and exclude deposit products.
comments.summary: UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights group, strongly opposes the proposal. It argues that the proposal would cut community development investment, raise thresholds that exempt many banks, restrict grants, keep assessment areas tied to branches, and exclude deposit products. It urges withdrawal and a modernization that adds race and ethnicity, digital and fintech activity, affordable deposit products, language access and community participation.
key_asks: Withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen CRA, jointly with the Federal Reserve.
Preserve CRA consideration for CD grants, keep CD obligations rigorous, and retain oversight of mid-sized banks.
Evaluate digital lending outside branch footprints, deposit products, race and ethnicity, language access, and community input in CRA exams.

provisions.quote: Exempting these institutions from more rigorous tests risks reducing accountability precisely where their lending and investment decisions can have substantial local consequences.
The agencies should preserve the CRA consideration for grants and ensure that the rules do not discourage banks from providing flexible support to trusted organizations
The agencies should evaluate whether banks offer low-cost, accessible and inclusive accounts
CRA examinations should evaluate lending where banks conduct substantial business, not only where they maintain branches.
The agencies should strengthen these mechanisms rather than rely primarily on bank-developed strategic plans and regulator-defined benchmarks.
UnidosUS urges the agencies to withdraw these changes and instead strengthen the CRA's ability to expand economic opportunities.
Setting the regulatory benchmark far below current levels would reset expectations for acceptable performance and weaken incentives for banks to maintain, let alone grow, current investments.

comments.summary: Scale Link, a nonprofit loan marketplace working with CDFIs and banks, opposes the OCC/FDIC proposal mainly because it would split CRA rules across regulators and weaken accountability. Remove asset thresholds entirely and hold all banks to large-bank tests and data reporting, rather than raising thresholds.
Do not adopt an indirect cost rate for CD grants; if one is adopted, treat 15% as a de minimis floor and use simple attestations, including a 60% assessment area attestation modeled on the CDFI Fund.

provisions.quote: Any new CRA rule should apply across all three regulators. If the OCC and FDIC cannot achieve that buy-in, the rule should not be changed.
the asset thresholds should not be moved higher and instead should be removed entirely. All banks should be held to the same tests and requirements as large banks.

Flexibility should be reserved only for those with an exemplary CRA track record.
It is not an undue burden to simply require all banks, regardless of size, to collect, maintain, and report on all the same data.
The list as written should remain.

comments.overall_quote: CDBA welcomes many of the proposed changes that provide greater flexibility and reduce regulatory burden for community banks.

Drop or substantially loosen the 15% CD grant administrative cost cap, sub-granting limits and Form 990/attestation requirements, and retain deposit services in the services test and the economic development purpose test

It cites local Ohio and HMDA data on the effects of higher asset thresholds, narrower evaluation of product lines, a weaker fair lending standard, looser infrastructure credit, omission of special purpose credit programs, and limits on CD grants. It also asks for a 60-day extension.
key_asks: Analyze the likely consequences for LMI communities before making changes, and allow comment on that analysis and evidence.
Extend the comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Continue to explicitly recognize special purpose credit programs, and consider all fair lending violations, including those from private enforcement, as grounds for a downgrade.

provisions.quote: Raising the asset threshold would considerably reduce CRA obligations and drastically weaken the incentive structure that motivates banks to provide loans and make investments in the communities that they serve.

The proposed CRA rules weakens the criteria for what constitutes evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices and would effectively give banks a pass on unlawful discrimination, redlining, and consumer protection.

Banks would have far fewer incentives to provide general operating funding, and many smaller and less resourced non-profits would be unable to meet the increased regulatory burden to receive these grants.
The OCC and FDIC should continue to explicitly recognize special purpose credit programs as responsive credit products under CRA.

comments.type_basis: LDF describes itself as the nation's premier racial justice law organization and focuses on redlining and discrimination in lending.
comments.overall_quote: LDF strongly urges the agencies to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.summary: LDF strongly opposes the proposal and urges its withdrawal. It argues the higher asset thresholds, the exclusion of deposit services from the service test, reduced data reporting and the narrower discriminatory-practices standard would deepen racial inequity in lending and violate the CRA's purpose. key_asks: Withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.
Withdraw the service test change and keep deposit services in the evaluation; retain the satisfactory CD performance requirement for intermediate banks.

a sole focus on credit services while excluding deposit services will likely lead to the failure of institutions meeting the needs of entire communities.
LDF opposes limiting consideration of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices to violations cited in public enforcement actions or judicial orders involving a Federal or State agency.
Raising the large-bank asset threshold would exempt additional banks from annual reporting of small-business lending data, making it harder for communities to identify credit gaps
The agencies give no reasoned basis for drastically changing the CRA regulations or adequately explain how the proposed changes account for these reliance interests.
The current proposed CRA rule omits SPCPs, which have proven to be quite beneficial for local communities

comments.name: National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders (NALCAB)
comments.type_basis: The letter describes NALCAB as a nonpartisan CDFI intermediary and national network serving over 200 economic development organizations.
comments.overall_quote: NALCAB is extremely concerned that the current proposed rule would allow many banks to sidestep responsibilities that expand access to capital and financial services in underserved communities.
comments.summary: NALCAB, a CDFI intermediary, supports several proposed additions (disaster resilience, credit for activities outside assessment areas, long-term CD investments, owner-occupied housing support) but strongly objects to the rule's weakening of accountability. It opposes the higher asset thresholds, the end of deposit-product evaluation for large banks, the dropped economic development purpose test, removal of complaint consideration and CD decoupling for intermediate banks, and the 15 percent cap on CD grant overhead.
key_asks: Withdraw the proposed CD grant overhead limit and preserve CRA consideration for grants, including operating support, to organizations with a community development purpose.
Maintain a framework that preserves accountability and keeps banks meeting credit and community development needs of underserved communities.
Retain the economic development purpose test and verification of actual community benefit rather than automatic qualification of intermediary activities.

provisions.quote: NALCAB is deeply concerned by the proposed changes to the asset size classifications for CRA-covered banks, which would reduce their accountability to local communities.
large banks would no longer be evaluated on whether their retail deposit products are affordable and accessible to low- and moderate-income consumers.
NALCAB also supports the agencies' proposal to allow banks to seek CRA credit for activities outside of their assessment areas.
NALCAB opposes the proposed changes of the definition of "economic development" activities under the CRA
A 15 percent cap fails to reflect the true cost of delivering these services.
Removing this requirement makes it more difficult for regulators and the public to assess whether local credit needs are being met
NALCAB opposes the proposed removal of consideration of written complaints in CRA evaluations of small and intermediate banks.
NALCAB supports the agencies' proposal to allow banks to receive CRA credit for activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and withstand natural disasters.
